claims.text: Controlling multi-metal precursor stoichiometry and low-temperature annealing promotes formation of a single-phase high-entropy alloy solid solution.
High mixing entropy promotes or stabilizes single-phase solid-solution formation in the five-noble-metal system.
Local lattice distortion is a cause of reliable single-phase formation during low-temperature annealing.
High-entropy alloys generally contain five or more elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic proportions.
Five noble-metal single-source precursors can form single-phase HEA nanoparticles at low temperature.
A hydrogen-containing reducing atmosphere is required for reliable final formation of the proposed five-metal solid solution.
Homogeneous atomic-level mixing induces local lattice distortions in the resulting solid solution.
The desired homogeneous solid solution is characterized by minimized mixing enthalpy and maximized entropy.
Electronic and geometric synergy among Pt, Pd, Rh, Ir, and Ru lowers catalytic reaction barriers.
The diversity of adsorption sites in an HEA improves adsorption-desorption behavior for multistep catalytic reactions.
Lattice distortion and ligand effects can modify the electronic properties of active sites and thereby improve catalytic performance.
Uniform lattice distortion creates stable, compositionally diverse active sites that increase catalytic turnover.
The five-component noble-metal catalyst will have higher catalytic activity than single-metal or binary-metal baselines.
The five-component noble-metal catalyst will be more stable than single-metal or binary-metal baselines.
In situ XRD and TEM will confirm formation of a single phase.
XPS will reveal a shift in the d-band center of the five-component material.
Pt-only nanoparticles lack the entropy-based stabilization, lattice-distortion effects, and active-site diversity of the five-component HEA.
The hypothesis applies only when the component metals have sufficiently low mixing enthalpy and form stable solid solutions below approximately 600 degrees Celsius under reducing conditions.
Large compositional disparities or highly immiscible constituents will favor phase separation or core-shell structures rather than a single phase.
Precursor-dependent phase inhomogeneity or partial segregation can reduce or eliminate catalytic synergy.
